title: A lotus at every name
hookLine: Vishnu offers Shiva a lotus for every name, and at the last name, the lotus is gone
carry: every name an offering, even from vishnu to shiva

cards: One lotus is missing. Vishnu has been kneeling before Shiva for a long time, saying a name and laying down a lotus, a name and a lotus, over and over. There should be a flower for every name.
Now, with one name left to say, his hand reaches into the basket and finds nothing. That's how the Shiva Purana tells it, and it's how that Purana frames its own list of Shiva's names.

teach.h: VISHNU: A NAME AND A LOTUS EACH.
teach.b: In the Shiva Purana, Vishnu needs Shiva's help. The demons are winning, so Vishnu goes to Shiva's shrine to honor him with a thousand names, a lotus at each one.
Shiva decides to test him, and quietly hides one lotus. So: the empty basket. What does Vishnu do?
Instead he remembers what people call him: Kamala-nayana, the lotus-eyed. His eyes are lotuses, he thinks, so he means to offer one of them.

As he reaches to take out his own eye, Shiva appears and stops him, delighted, and gives him a gift: the Sudarshana, the blazing discus Vishnu carries from then on. Hindus keep this story for two reasons.
First, it shows what a name is for.
In Hindu worship, saying God's name is itself an offering. In an archana at a temple, the priest says a name and lays down a flower, a name and a flower, the way Vishnu did.

Each name was a gift, so when the flowers ran out, Vishnu gave himself. Second, look at who's kneeling. Vishnu, the great god of one huge family of Hindus, worshipping Shiva, the great god of another, with no one shamed.
Many teachers read stories like this as a quiet warning against turning the gods into rival teams.
Plenty of Hindu homes keep both on one shelf, and some temples show them as one figure, half Vishnu and half Shiva: Harihara.
So if your family's shelf is all Krishna and your grandmother goes to Shiva's temple on Mondays, nobody is switching sides. Vishnu got there first.

how: Hindus tell this story of Vishnu's lotuses in the Shiva Purana, and in a Shiva temple a devotee may sponsor an archana in which a flower is offered at each of Shiva's names.

games.q: you're Vishnu. you've offered a lotus at every one of Shiva's names. one name is left, and the basket is empty. what do you do?
o: say the last name without a flower; it's close enough.
offer one of your own eyes, since they call you lotus-eyed.
games.why: Vishnu reaches to give his own eye. Shiva appears, stops him, and gives him the Sudarshana discus.

practice: Pick a name of God you love, Shiva, Krishna, the Goddess, or simply God, and say it silently once on each out-breath, as if you were laying down a flower each time.

When your mind wanders, that's your empty basket: just come back and give the next name, the latest as real as the first. If you don't pray, offer one thing you're grateful for on each breath instead.

wordCard.voice: The Shiva Sahasranama. Today's selection: the Shiva Purana's story of Vishnu offering a lotus at every name, and his own eye when one went missing.
